definition: A device that turns something about the world into a number your program can read.
A device that moves or changes the world, like a motor.
A value that changes over time and carries information.
A signal that can take any value in a range, like a voltage between 0 and 5 volts.
A signal with only two states, high or low.
The smallest change a sensor can report.
How close a reading is to the true value, on average.
How close repeated readings are to each other.
Random variation in a reading that has nothing to do with what is being measured.
How often a sensor takes a new measurement.
How often your program asks for a reading.
The Brain's 3-wire ports, lettered A to H, for simple digital and analog sensors. Short for analog-digital interface.
A reading that slowly moves away from the truth even though nothing happened.
A sensor that knows its value right away, with no need for a starting point.
A sensor that only knows how much has changed since it started counting.
Measuring a sensor against something known so its readings can be trusted or corrected.
A switch whose contacts are apart until it is pressed.
A resistor that holds a wire high until something connects it to ground.
The rapid on-off chatter of metal contacts as they close.
Moving a mechanism to a known position, usually a switch, so a relative sensor has a true zero.
A sensor that measures how far a shaft has turned.
The smallest step an encoder can count. On a blue V5 motor one tick is 1.2 degrees of shaft.
How many ticks an encoder counts in one full turn of its shaft. For a V5 motor it depends on the cartridge.
The teeth on the driving gear divided by the teeth on the driven gear, which is how many turns the driven gear makes for each turn of the driving one.
The distance around a wheel, which is how far it rolls in one turn.
The small gap between gear teeth, which lets one turn a little before the other moves.
A wheel turning without the robot moving the matching distance.
The encoder built into every V5 motor, which reports its shaft angle over the motor's Smart Port. Often shortened to IME.
Two signals a quarter cycle apart, whose order tells which way a shaft is turning.
An encoder that counts light passing through slots in a spinning wheel.
An encoder that measures a shaft's angle from a magnetic field.
One hundredth of a degree: the unit the rotation sensor reports in, not a statement of how finely it can measure.
An encoder that knows the shaft's angle as soon as it powers on.
A variable resistor that turns a shaft angle into a voltage.
Two resistances in series, where the voltage between them depends on their ratio.
An analog-to-digital converter, which turns a voltage into a whole number.
A part of a sensor's travel where it can't give a useful reading.
An inertial measurement unit, a sensor that combines a gyroscope and an accelerometer.
A sensor that measures how fast it is rotating.
A sensor that measures acceleration, including gravity.
Which way the robot faces, as an angle from 0 up to 360.
Rotation about the vertical axis, like a robot turning on the field.
Rotation that tips the nose up or down.
Rotation that tips the robot to one side.
Error that builds up when small errors in a rate are added over time.
A value jumping back to the start of its range, like a heading going from 359 to 0.
Measuring distance by timing how long a pulse takes to reach something and come back.
The area a sensor can see.
A number a sensor reports about how much to trust its reading.
A number reserved to mean something special, like 9999 meaning nothing was detected, instead of a real measurement.
Replacing each reading with the middle value of the last few, so one wild reading can't move the result.
A color given as an angle around a color wheel.
How strong a color is, from gray to vivid.
A sensor that tells how close an object is, without measuring an exact distance.
A color given as amounts of red, green and blue.
The light already in the room, as opposed to the sensor's own.
Recognizing the direction an object moves across a sensor.
